newsitem.title: DENMARK: Carlsberg profits up but share down.
newsitem.headline: Carlsberg profits up but share down.

text.p: Danish brewer Carlsberg on Tuesday reported first half 1996/1997 sales and profits up but the local stock market was unimpressed and sent the firm's share down.

The firm's report for the six months to March 31, 1997 showed pre-tax profit up to 870 million crowns ($132.2 million) from 741 million the year before and turnover up to 9.21 billion crowns from 8.54 billion.
Analysts had on average forecast pre-tax profit of 812 million crowns and turnover of 8.99 billion.
But Carlsberg said that the results were largely due to the stronger British pound and an increased stake in Swedish brewer Falcon, to 50 percent from 30 percent.

"Carlsberg's interim operating profit is somewhat disappointing. The pre-tax result was saved by financial items, the share looks like falling moderately on the result," a dealer told Reuters shortly after publication of the report.
The share closed on Tuesday at 388.00 crowns, down seven crowns from Monday's close and off an earlier high of 399.00.
An analyst, who asked not to be named, said that Carlsberg was suffering short-term from poor growth in China, where it has heavy investment programmes.

"China is costing Carlsberg a lot of money and this is dragging its performance in Asia down. This affects operating results initially, although in the longer term the investment in China should prove sensible," he said.
In Tuesday's report Carlsberg said that Carslberg-Tetley, which it jointly owns with Britain's Bass, had a first-half result similar to that of the year before but it gave no figure.
Bass seeks to buy Carlsberg's half of the British-based joint venture, thereby becoming Britain's largest brewer, but is awaiting clearance from U.K. regulators.
"In view of the authorities' lengthy investigations and the resulting uncertainty among employees and customers, the result in the U.K. is considered highly satisfactory," the Carlsberg report said.

It added that 84 percent of Carlsberg group sales were abroad, while at home in Denmark, where Carlsberg has around 82 percent of the market, total beer consumption fell by 0.3 percent year-on-year over the reporting period.
Neverthless, it added, the share for its Carlsberg and Tuborg brands increased although share fell at the lower end of the market, where its Wiibroe brand operates.
Domestic soft-drink sales rose by 8.6 percent, led by Coca-Cola products, which Carlsberg bottles and distributes.

The two partners are seeking approval from European Union competition authorities to extend the alliance to Sweden, and eventually throughout the Nordic and Baltic region, in a jointly-owned company named Coca-Cola Nordic Beverages (CCNB).
Finnish beverages group Oy Hartwall said on Tuesday that its agreement to produce, sell and distribute Coca-Cola products locally would expire at the end of 1998.
Analysts expect CCNB to take up the license from 1999, bringing in Carlsberg's existing Finnish partner Sinebrychoff.
